question.prompt:
A corner of a tiled floor is shown. If the entire floor is tiled in this way and each of the four corners looks like this one, then what fraction of the tiled floor is made of darker tiles?

[Figure 1](figures/2002_AMC_8_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The pattern repeats every six rows and every six columns, so we can measure one complete repeating block instead of the entire floor. Use the six-by-six block beginning at the shown upper-left corner. The matching pattern at all four corners means the floor ends at corresponding block boundaries, so it consists of complete blocks of this kind.

Take one small grid square as one unit of area. In the block, the dark areas in the six rows, from top to bottom, are
\[
1,\quad2,\quad5,\quad5,\quad2,\quad1.
\]
For example, the first row contains two dark half-squares, totaling \(1\), and the third row contains four full dark squares and two dark half-squares, totaling \(5\). Each half-square is a triangle formed by a diagonal, so it has half the area of its square. Counting by rows includes every dark piece once.

The block therefore has dark area
\[
1+2+5+5+2+1=16
\]
out of total area \(6\cdot6=36\). Every block has the same fraction of dark area, so the entire floor has dark fraction
\[
\frac{16}{36}=\boxed{\frac49},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
solutions.title: Count the dark area in one repeating block
